John C. Calhoun was the seventh Vice President of the United States, serving under John Quincy Adams from eighteen twenty-five to eighteen twenty-nine and under Andrew Jackson from eighteen twenty-nine to eighteen thirty-two. Though he served as Vice President to two presidents, he left office to pursue a Senate career where he wielded greater influence and became one of the leading political and intellectual voices of the antebellum South. Before his vice presidency, Calhoun served as Secretary of War under President James Monroe, overseeing military expansion and the acquisition of Spanish Florida. A prominent nationalist early in his career, Calhoun later pivoted to become the South's most eloquent defender of slavery and states' rights. He authored the South Carolina Exposition and Protest in eighteen twenty-eight, which became the theoretical foundation for the doctrine of nullification—the idea that states could reject federal laws they deemed unconstitutional. This theory led to the Nullification Crisis from eighteen thirty-two to eighteen thirty-three when South Carolina threatened to secede over the Tariff of Abominations, nearly precipitating civil war a generation before Fort Sumter. Known for his piercing intellect and oratorical power, Calhoun's speeches on slavery and constitutional theory profoundly influenced Southern political thought. He served in the Senate for seventeen years, making him one of the most powerful congressional figures of his era.
